CHAPTER 2. Scene IAct Ihttps://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare/pericles/text/act-1#scene-1-1

Antioch. A room in the palace.

Enter Antiochus, Prince Pericles, and followers.

Antiochus

Young prince of Tyre, you have at large received

The danger of the task you undertake.

Pericles

I have, Antiochus, and, with a soul

Embolden'd with the glory of her praise,

Think death no hazard in this enterprise.

Antiochus

Bring in our daughter, clothed like a bride,

For the embracements even of Jove himself;

At whose conception, till Lucina reign'd,

Nature this dowry gave, to glad her presence,

The senate-house of planets all did sit,

To knit in her their best perfections.

Music. Enter the Daughter of Antiochus.

Pericles

See where she comes, apparell'd like the spring,

Graces her subjects, and her thoughts the king

Of every virtue gives renown to men!

Her face the book of praises, where is read

Nothing but curious pleasures, as from thence

Sorrow were ever razed, and testy wrath

Could never be her mild companion.

You gods that made me man, and sway in love,

That have inflamed desire in my breast

To taste the fruit of yon celestial tree,

Or die in the adventure, be my helps,

As I am son and servant to your will,

To compass such a boundless happiness!

Antiochus Prince Pericles⁠--

Pericles That would be son to great Antiochus.

Antiochus

Before thee stands this fair Hesperides,

With golden fruit, but dangerous to be touch'd;

For death-like dragons here affright thee hard:

Her face, like heaven, enticeth thee to view

Her countless glory, which desert must gain;

And which, without desert, because thine eye

Presumes to reach, all thy whole heap must die.

Yon sometimes famous princes, like thyself,

Drawn by report, adventurous by desire,

Tell thee, with speechless tongues and semblance pale,

That without covering, save yon field of stars,

Here they stand martyrs, slain in Cupid's wars;

And with dead cheeks advise thee to desist

For going on death's net, whom none resist.

Pericles

Antiochus, I thank thee, who hath taught

My frail mortality to know itself,

And by those fearful objects to prepare

This body, like to them, to what I must;

For death remember'd should be like a mirror,

Who tells us life's but breath, to trust it error.

I'll make my will then, and, as sick men do

Who know the world, see heaven, but, feeling woe,

Gripe not at earthly joys as erst they did;

So I bequeath a happy peace to you

And all good men, as every prince should do;

My riches to the earth from whence they came;

But my unspotted fire of love to you. To the Daughter of Antiochus.

Thus ready for the way of life or death,

I wait the sharpest blow, Antiochus.

Antiochus

Scorning advice, read the conclusion then:

Which read and not expounded, 'tis decreed,

As these before thee thou thyself shalt bleed.

Daughter

Of all say'd yet, mayst thou prove prosperous!

Of all say'd yet, I wish thee happiness!

Pericles

Like a bold champion, I assume the lists,

Nor ask advice of any other thought

But faithfulness and courage.

He reads the riddle.

I am no viper, yet I feed

On mother's flesh which did me breed.

I sought a husband, in which labour

I found that kindness in a father:

He's father, son, and husband mild;

I mother, wife, and yet his child.

How they may be, and yet in two,

As you will live, resolve it you.

Sharp physic is the last: but, O you powers

That give heaven countless eyes to view men's acts,

Why cloud they not their sights perpetually,

If this be true, which makes me pale to read it?

Fair glass of light, I loved you, and could still, Takes hold of the hand of the Princess.

Were not this glorious casket stored with ill:

But I must tell you, now my thoughts revolt;

For he's no man on whom perfections wait

That, knowing sin within, will touch the gate.

You are a fair viol, and your sense the strings;

Who, finger'd to make man his lawful music,

Would draw heaven down, and all the gods, to hearken;

But being play'd upon before your time,

Hell only danceth at so harsh a chime.

Good sooth, I care not for you.

Antiochus

Prince Pericles, touch not, upon thy life,

For that's an article within our law,

As dangerous as the rest. Your time's expired:

Either expound now, or receive your sentence.

Pericles

Great king,

Few love to hear the sins they love to act;

'Twould braid yourself too near for me to tell it.

Who has a book of all that monarchs do,

He's more secure to keep it shut than shown:

For vice repeated is like the wandering wind,

Blows dust in other's eyes, to spread itself;

And yet the end of all is bought thus dear,

The breath is gone, and the sore eyes see clear

To stop the air would hurt them. The blind mole casts

Copp'd hills towards heaven, to tell the earth is throng'd

By man's oppression; and the poor worm doth die for't.

Kings are earth's gods; in vice their law's their will;

And if Jove stray, who dares say Jove doth ill?

It is enough you know; and it is fit,

What being more known grows worse, to smother it.

All love the womb that their first being bred,

Then give my tongue like leave to love my head.

Antiochus

Aside. Heaven, that I had thy head! he has found the meaning:

But I will gloze with him.⁠--Young prince of Tyre,

Though by the tenour of our strict edict,

Your exposition misinterpreting,

We might proceed to cancel of your days;

Yet hope, succeeding from so fair a tree

As your fair self, doth tune us otherwise:

Forty days longer we do respite you;

If by which time our secret be undone,

This mercy shows we'll joy in such a son:

And until then your entertain shall be

As doth befit our honour and your worth. Exeunt all but Pericles.

Pericles

How courtesy would seem to cover sin,

When what is done is like an hypocrite,

The which is good in nothing but in sight!

If it be true that I interpret false,

Then were it certain you were not so bad

As with foul incest to abuse your soul;

Where now you're both a father and a son,

By your untimely claspings with your child,

Which pleasure fits an husband, not a father;

And she an eater of her mother's flesh,

By the defiling of her parent's bed;

And both like serpents are, who though they feed

On sweetest flowers, yet they poison breed.

Antioch, farewell! for wisdom sees, those men

Blush not in actions blacker than the night,

Will shun no course to keep them from the light.

One sin, I know, another doth provoke;

Murder's as near to lust as flame to smoke:

Poison and treason are the hands of sin,

Ay, and the targets, to put off the shame:

Then, lest my life be cropp'd to keep you clear,

By flight I'll shun the danger which I fear. Exit.

Reenter Antiochus.

Antiochus

He hath found the meaning, for which we mean

To have his head.

He must not live to trumpet forth my infamy,

Nor tell the world Antiochus doth sin

In such a loathed manner;

And therefore instantly this prince must die;

For by his fall my honour must keep high.

Who attends us there?

Enter Thaliard.

Thaliard Doth your highness call?

Antiochus

Thaliard,

You are of our chamber, and our mind partakes

Her private actions to your secrecy;

And for your faithfulness we will advance you.

Thaliard, behold, here's poison, and here's gold;

We hate the prince of Tyre, and thou must kill him:

It fits thee not to ask the reason why,

Because we bid it. Say, is it done?

Thaliard

My lord,

'Tis done.

Antiochus Enough.

Enter a Messenger.

Let your breath cool yourself, telling your haste.

Messenger My lord, prince Pericles is fled. Exit.

Antiochus

As thou

Wilt live, fly after: and like an arrow shot

From a well-experienced archer hits the mark

His eye doth level at, so thou ne'er return

Unless thou say "Prince Pericles is dead."

Thaliard

My lord,

If I can get him within my pistol's length,

I'll make him sure enough: so, farewell to your highness.

Antiochus

Thaliard, adieu! Exit Thaliard. Till Pericles be dead,

My heart can lend no succour to my head. Exit.

questions.question: What warning does Antiochus give Pericles before the trial?
questions.questionKo: 안티오코스는 시험에 앞서 페리클레스에게 어떤 경고를 하는가?

options.text: Before him stands a fair Hesperides with golden fruit, dangerous to be touched — and famous princes before him stand as martyrs, advising him with dead cheeks to desist.
options.textKo: 그 앞에 황금 열매의 헤스페리데스가 서 있으나 손대면 위험하다고 — 그를 앞서 온 이름난 왕자들이 순교자로 서서, 죽은 뺨으로 그만두라 이르고 있다고.

options.text: That the task may be attempted only once in a lifetime.
options.textKo: 그 과업은 평생 한 번만 시도할 수 있다고.

options.text: That his daughter has already been promised elsewhere.
options.textKo: 딸이 이미 다른 데 약속되었다고.

options.text: That the gods forbid strangers to woo in Antioch.
options.textKo: 신들이 안티오크에서 이방인의 구애를 금한다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: Before thee stands this fair Hesperides, With golden fruit, but dangerous to be touch’d

questions.question: How does Pericles answer that warning?
questions.questionKo: 페리클레스는 그 경고에 어떻게 답하는가?

options.text: He asks for a day’s delay to consider.
options.textKo: 하루만 생각할 말미를 달라 청한다.

options.text: He thanks Antiochus for teaching his frail mortality to know itself — death remembered should be like a mirror, which tells us life is but breath, and to trust it error.
options.textKo: 연약한 필멸의 몸이 제 처지를 알게 해 주어 고맙다고 — 죽음을 기억하는 것은 거울과 같아, 삶이란 숨결일 뿐이며 그것을 믿는 것이 잘못임을 알려 준다고.

options.text: He mocks the warning as a trick to frighten suitors.
options.textKo: 구혼자를 겁주려는 속임수라 비웃는다.

options.text: He turns and leaves the court at once.
options.textKo: 곧바로 돌아서서 궁을 나선다.

questions.sourceSnippet: For death remember’d should be like a mirror, Who tells us life’s but breath, to trust it error

questions.question: What are the terms of the trial Pericles undertakes?
questions.questionKo: 페리클레스가 떠맡은 시험의 조건은?

options.text: He must fight the king’s champion in the lists.
options.textKo: 왕의 투사와 결투장에서 싸워야 한다.

options.text: He must bring a dowry equal to the kingdom.
options.textKo: 왕국에 맞먹는 지참금을 가져와야 한다.

options.text: He must read the conclusion and expound it — read and not expounded, it is decreed he shall bleed as those before him.
options.textKo: 결론을 읽고 풀이해야 한다 — 읽고도 풀지 못하면 앞선 이들처럼 피를 흘리기로 정해져 있다.

options.text: He must serve one year at Antioch before he may speak.
options.textKo: 말을 꺼내기 전에 안티오크에서 일 년을 섬겨야 한다.

questions.sourceSnippet: Which read and not expounded, ’tis decreed, As these before thee thou thyself shalt bleed

questions.question: Why does Pericles refuse to speak his answer aloud?
questions.questionKo: 페리클레스는 왜 제 답을 소리 내어 말하지 않는가?

options.text: Because he does not in fact know the answer.
options.textKo: 실은 답을 모르기 때문에.

options.text: Because the law forbids the answer to be spoken.
options.textKo: 법이 답을 입 밖에 내는 것을 금하기 때문에.

options.text: Because he wishes to marry the daughter regardless.
options.textKo: 그래도 딸과 혼인하고 싶기 때문에.

options.text: Few love to hear the sins they love to act — he who has a book of all that monarchs do is more secure to keep it shut than shown.
options.textKo: 저지르기 좋아하는 죄를 듣기 좋아하는 이는 드물다며 — 군주들이 한 일을 다 적은 책을 가진 자는 펼치기보다 닫아 두는 편이 안전하다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: Few love to hear the sins they love to act

questions.question: What does Pericles say about kings and their law?
questions.questionKo: 페리클레스는 왕과 그 법에 대해 무엇이라 말하는가?

options.text: Kings are earth’s gods; in vice their law’s their will — and if Jove stray, who dares say Jove doth ill?
options.textKo: 왕은 땅 위의 신이라, 악행에서는 그 뜻이 곧 법이라고 — 유피테르가 어긋난들 누가 감히 유피테르가 잘못했다 하겠느냐고.

options.text: That kings must answer to the senate like other men.
options.textKo: 왕도 다른 이들처럼 원로원에 답해야 한다고.

options.text: That a king who sins loses his crown by law.
options.textKo: 죄지은 왕은 법에 따라 왕관을 잃는다고.

options.text: That the gods punish kings first and hardest.
options.textKo: 신들은 왕을 가장 먼저 가장 무겁게 벌한다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: Kings are earth’s gods; in vice their law’s their will

questions.question: What does Antiochus grant Pericles, and what does he say aside?
questions.questionKo: 안티오코스가 페리클레스에게 내리는 것과, 방백으로 하는 말은?

options.text: His daughter’s hand, and aside he blesses the match.
options.textKo: 딸의 손 — 방백으로 그 혼사를 축복한다.

options.text: Forty days’ respite, framed as mercy — while aside he says "he has found the meaning: but I will gloze with him."
options.textKo: 자비인 양 꾸민 40일의 유예 — 방백으로는 "그가 뜻을 알아냈구나. 그러나 나는 그를 구슬리겠다" 고 한다.

options.text: Immediate execution, and aside he regrets it.
options.textKo: 즉각적인 처형 — 방백으로 후회한다.

options.text: Safe conduct home, and aside he wishes him well.
options.textKo: 무사히 돌아갈 통행 허가 — 방백으로 잘되기를 빈다.

questions.sourceSnippet: Forty days longer we do respite you

questions.question: What does Antiochus give Thaliard, and what happens next?
questions.questionKo: 안티오코스가 탈리아드에게 준 것과, 그다음에 벌어지는 일은?

options.text: A letter of pardon to carry to Tyre.
options.textKo: 티레로 가져갈 사면장.

options.text: Command of the fleet, to blockade Tyre’s harbour.
options.textKo: 티레 항구를 봉쇄할 함대의 지휘권.

options.text: Poison and gold, with the charge to kill the prince of Tyre — then a messenger reports that Pericles is fled, and Thaliard is sent after him.
options.textKo: 독과 금, 그리고 티레의 왕자를 죽이라는 명 — 이어 전령이 페리클레스가 달아났다 알리자 탈리아드를 뒤쫓아 보낸다.

options.text: Nothing — he changes his mind and lets Pericles go.
options.textKo: 아무것도 — 마음을 바꾸어 페리클레스를 보내 준다.

questions.sourceSnippet: behold, here’s poison, and here’s gold

chapters.content:
CHAPTER 3. Scene IIAct Ihttps://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare/pericles/text/act-1#scene-1-2

Tyre. A room in the palace.

Enter Pericles.

Pericles

To Lords without. Let none disturb us.⁠--Why should this change of thoughts,

The sad companion, dull-eyed melancholy,

Be my so used a guest as not an hour,

In the day's glorious walk, or peaceful night,

The tomb where grief should sleep, can breed me quiet?

Here pleasures court mine eyes, and mine eyes shun them,

And danger, which I fear'd, is at Antioch,

Whose aim seems far too short to hit me here:

Yet neither pleasure's art can joy my spirits,

Nor yet the other's distance comfort me.

Then it is thus: the passions of the mind,

That have their first conception by mis-dread,

Have after-nourishment and life by care;

And what was first but fear what might be done,

Grows elder now and cares it be not done.

And so with me: the great Antiochus,

'Gainst whom I am too little to contend,

Since he's so great can make his will his act,

Will think me speaking, though I swear to silence;

Nor boots it me to say I honour him,

If he suspect I may dishonour him:

And what may make him blush in being known,

He'll stop the course by which it might be known;

With hostile forces he'll o'erspread the land,

And with the ostent of war will look so huge,

Amazement shall drive courage from the state;

Our men be vanquish'd ere they do resist,

And subjects punish'd that ne'er thought offence:

Which care of them, not pity of myself,

Who am no more but as the tops of trees,

Which fence the roots they grow by and defend them,

Makes both my body pine and soul to languish,

And punish that before that he would punish.

Enter Helicanus, with other Lords.

First Lord Joy and all comfort in your sacred breast!

Second Lord

And keep your mind, till you return to us,

Peaceful and comfortable!

Helicanus

Peace, peace, and give experience tongue.

They do abuse the king that flatter him:

For flattery is the bellows blows up sin;

The thing which is flatter'd, but a spark,

To which that blast gives heat and stronger glowing;

Whereas reproof, obedient and in order,

Fits kings, as they are men, for they may err.

When Signior Sooth here does proclaim a peace,

He flatters you, makes war upon your life.

Prince, pardon me, or strike me, if you please;

I cannot be much lower than my knees.

Pericles

All leave us else; but let your cares o'erlook

What shipping and what lading's in our haven,

And then return to us. Exeunt Lords. Helicanus, thou

Hast moved us: what seest thou in our looks?

Helicanus An angry brow, dread lord.

Pericles

If there be such a dart in princes' frowns,

How durst thy tongue move anger to our face?

Helicanus

How dare the plants look up to heaven, from whence

They have their nourishment?

Pericles

Thou know'st I have power

To take thy life from thee.

Helicanus

Kneeling. I have ground the axe myself;

Do you but strike the blow.

Pericles

Rise, prithee, rise.

Sit down: thou art no flatterer:

I thank thee for it; and heaven forbid

That kings should let their ears hear their faults hid!

Fit counsellor and servant for a prince,

Who by thy wisdom makest a prince thy servant,

What wouldst thou have me do?

Helicanus

To bear with patience

Such griefs as you yourself do lay upon yourself.

Pericles

Thou speak'st like a physician, Helicanus,

That minister'st a potion unto me

That thou wouldst tremble to receive thyself.

Attend me, then: I went to Antioch,

Where as thou know'st, against the face of death,

I sought the purchase of a glorious beauty,

From whence an issue I might propagate,

Are arms to princes, and bring joys to subjects.

Her face was to mine eye beyond all wonder;

The rest⁠--hark in thine ear⁠--as black as incest:

Which by my knowledge found, the sinful father

Seem'd not to strike, but smooth: but thou know'st this,

'Tis time to fear when tyrants seem to kiss.

Such fear so grew in me, I hither fled,

Under the covering of a careful night,

Who seem'd my good protector; and, being here,

Bethought me what was past, what might succeed.

I knew him tyrannous; and tyrants' fears

Decrease not, but grow faster than the years:

And should he doubt it, as no doubt he doth,

That I should open to the listening air

How many worthy princes' bloods were shed,

To keep his bed of blackness unlaid ope,

To lop that doubt, he'll fill this land with arms,

And make pretence of wrong that I have done him;

When all, for mine, if I may call offence,

Must feel war's blow, who spares not innocence:

Which love to all, of which thyself art one,

Who now reprovest me for it⁠--

Helicanus Alas, sir!

Pericles

Drew sleep out of mine eyes, blood from my cheeks,

Musings into my mind, with thousand doubts

How I might stop this tempest ere it came;

And finding little comfort to relieve them,

I thought it princely charity to grieve them.

Helicanus

Well, my lord, since you have given me leave to speak,

Freely will I speak. Antiochus you fear,

And justly too, I think, you fear the tyrant,

Who either by public war or private treason

Will take away your life.

Therefore, my lord, go travel for a while,

Till that his rage and anger be forgot,

Or till the Destinies do cut his thread of life.

Your rule direct to any; if to me,

Day serves not light more faithful than I'll be.

Pericles

I do not doubt thy faith;

But should he wrong my liberties in my absence?

Helicanus

We'll mingle our bloods together in the earth,

From whence we had our being and our birth.

Pericles

Tyre, I now look from thee then, and to Tarsus

Intend my travel, where I'll hear from thee;

And by whose letters I'll dispose myself.

The care I had and have of subjects' good

On thee I lay whose wisdom's strength can bear it.

I'll take thy word for faith, not ask thine oath:

Who shuns not to break one will sure crack both:

But in our orbs we'll live so round and safe,

That time of both this truth shall ne'er convince,

Thou show'dst a subject's shine, I a true prince. Exeunt.

questions.question: How does Pericles describe the growth of his fear?
questions.questionKo: 페리클레스는 제 두려움이 자라는 과정을 어떻게 말하는가?

options.text: That fear leaves a man the moment danger is distant.
options.textKo: 위험이 멀어지는 순간 두려움은 떠난다고.

options.text: That fear is a stranger to princes by nature.
options.textKo: 두려움은 본디 왕자에게 낯선 것이라고.

options.text: That only pleasure can drive out fear.
options.textKo: 오직 쾌락만이 두려움을 몰아낸다고.

options.text: Passions first conceived by mis-dread have after-nourishment and life by care — what was first but fear what might be done grows elder and cares it be not done.
options.textKo: 잘못된 겁에서 잉태된 정념은 근심으로 자라난다고 — 처음에는 무슨 일이 일어날까 하는 두려움이던 것이 자라나, 그 일이 일어나지 않게 하려 애쓰게 된다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: That have their first conception by mis-dread, Have after-nourishment and life by care

questions.question: Why does Pericles fear Antiochus even though he swears silence?
questions.questionKo: 침묵을 맹세했음에도 페리클레스가 안티오코스를 두려워하는 까닭은?

options.text: Antiochus is so great he can make his will his act, and will think Pericles speaking however he swears — and what would make him blush in being known, he will stop the course by which it might be known.
options.textKo: 안티오코스는 뜻을 곧 행위로 만들 만큼 강대해, 무엇을 맹세하든 페리클레스가 발설하리라 여길 것이며 — 알려지면 낯 뜨거울 일이라면 알려질 길 자체를 막으리라는 것.

options.text: Because Antiochus has already sent an army to Tyre.
options.textKo: 이미 티레로 군대를 보냈으므로.

options.text: Because the gods have warned him in a dream.
options.textKo: 신들이 꿈으로 경고했으므로.

options.text: Because Helicanus advised him that war is certain.
options.textKo: 헬리카누스가 전쟁이 확실하다 조언했으므로.

questions.sourceSnippet: Since he’s so great can make his will his act

questions.question: What does Helicanus say about flattery?
questions.questionKo: 헬리카누스는 아첨에 대해 무엇이라 하는가?

options.text: That flattery is harmless if the king knows it for what it is.
options.textKo: 왕이 아첨인 줄 알기만 하면 해롭지 않다고.

options.text: Flattery is the bellows that blows up sin — the thing flattered is but a spark, to which that blast gives heat and stronger glowing.
options.textKo: 아첨은 죄를 부풀리는 풀무라고 — 아첨받는 것은 불티일 뿐인데, 그 바람이 열과 더 센 불빛을 준다고.

options.text: That a counsellor must flatter to keep his place.
options.textKo: 조언자는 자리를 지키려면 아첨해야 한다고.

options.text: That flattery is the only way to soothe a grieving prince.
options.textKo: 슬퍼하는 왕자를 달랠 길은 아첨뿐이라고.

questions.sourceSnippet: For flattery is the bellows blows up sin

questions.question: How does Helicanus answer when Pericles says he has power to take his life?
questions.questionKo: 목숨을 거둘 힘이 있다는 페리클레스의 말에 헬리카누스는 어떻게 답하는가?

options.text: He begs pardon and takes back everything he said.
options.textKo: 용서를 빌며 한 말을 모두 거둔다.

options.text: He says the lords of Tyre would never permit it.
options.textKo: 티레의 귀족들이 결코 허락하지 않으리라 한다.

options.text: He kneels and says he has ground the axe himself — the prince need only strike the blow.
options.textKo: 무릎 꿇고 도끼는 자기가 직접 갈아 두었으니 왕자는 내리치기만 하면 된다고 한다.

options.text: He flees the chamber without answering.
options.textKo: 답하지 않고 방을 빠져나간다.

questions.sourceSnippet: I have ground the axe myself; Do you but strike the blow

questions.question: What does Pericles conclude about a prince and his counsellors?
questions.questionKo: 페리클레스가 왕자와 조언자에 대해 내리는 결론은?

options.text: That a prince should hear only those who agree with him.
options.textKo: 왕자는 자기와 뜻이 같은 이만 들어야 한다고.

options.text: That counsellors should speak only when asked.
options.textKo: 조언자는 물을 때만 말해야 한다고.

options.text: That no subject may kneel while giving counsel.
options.textKo: 조언하며 무릎 꿇는 신하는 있을 수 없다고.

options.text: Heaven forbid that kings should let their ears hear their faults hid — such a counsellor by his wisdom makes a prince his servant.
options.textKo: 왕이 제 허물을 감춘 채 듣게 되는 일이 없기를 — 그런 조언자는 지혜로써 왕자를 제 종으로 만든다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: And heaven forbid That kings should let their ears hear their faults hid!

questions.question: What advice does Helicanus give once permitted to speak freely?
questions.questionKo: 터놓고 말해도 좋다는 허락을 받은 헬리카누스의 조언은?

options.text: Go travel for a while, till Antiochus’s rage be forgot or the Destinies cut his thread of life — and direct the rule to anyone he chooses.
options.textKo: 안티오코스의 분노가 잊히거나 운명의 여신들이 그 목숨의 실을 끊을 때까지 얼마간 여행하라고 — 그리고 통치는 누구에게든 맡기라고.

options.text: Raise an army and strike Antioch first.
options.textKo: 군대를 일으켜 안티오크를 먼저 치라고.

options.text: Send an embassy to Antioch to sue for peace.
options.textKo: 안티오크에 사절을 보내 화친을 청하라고.

options.text: Stay in Tyre and fortify the harbour.
options.textKo: 티레에 남아 항구를 요새로 만들라고.

questions.sourceSnippet: Therefore, my lord, go travel for a while

questions.question: What does Pericles decide at the end of the scene?
questions.questionKo: 장면 끝에서 페리클레스가 정하는 것은?

options.text: To go to Antioch and confront the king openly.
options.textKo: 안티오크로 가서 왕과 정면으로 맞서기로.

options.text: To travel to Tarsus, laying the care of his subjects on Helicanus — taking his word for faith, not asking his oath.
options.textKo: 타르수스로 떠나며 백성을 돌보는 일을 헬리카누스에게 맡기기로 — 맹세를 요구하지 않고 그의 말만 믿기로.

options.text: To abdicate and give the crown to Escanes.
options.textKo: 왕위에서 물러나 왕관을 에스카네스에게 주기로.

options.text: To remain in Tyre and await Antiochus’s move.
options.textKo: 티레에 남아 안티오코스의 다음 수를 기다리기로.

questions.sourceSnippet: I’ll take thy word for faith, not ask thine oath

chapters.content:
CHAPTER 4. Scene IIIAct Ihttps://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare/pericles/text/act-1#scene-1-3

Tyre. An ante-chamber in the palace.

Enter Thaliard.

Thaliard So, this is Tyre, and this the court. Here must I kill King Pericles; and if I do it not, I am sure to be hanged at home: 'tis dangerous. Well, I perceive he was a wise fellow, and had good discretion, that, being bid to ask what he would of the king, desired he might know none of his secrets: now do I see he had some reason for't; for if a king bid a man be a villain, he's bound by the indenture of his oath to be one. Hush! here come the lords of Tyre.

Enter Helicanus and Escanes, with other Lords of Tyre.

Helicanus

You shall not need, my fellow peers of Tyre,

Further to question me of your king's departure:

His seal'd commission, left in trust with me,

Doth speak sufficiently he's gone to travel.

Thaliard Aside. How! the king gone!

Helicanus

If further yet you will be satisfied,

Why, as it were unlicensed of your loves,

He would depart, I'll give some light unto you.

Being at Antioch⁠--

Thaliard Aside. What from Antioch?

Helicanus

Royal Antiochus⁠--on what cause I know not⁠--

Took some displeasure at him; at least he judged so:

And doubting lest that he had err'd or sinn'd,

To show his sorrow, he'ld correct himself;

So puts himself unto the shipman's toil,

With whom each minute threatens life or death.

Thaliard

Aside. Well, I perceive

I shall not be hang'd now, although I would;

But since he's gone, the king's seas must please:

He 'scaped the land, to perish at the sea.

I'll present myself. Peace to the lords of Tyre!

Helicanus Lord Thaliard from Antiochus is welcome.

Thaliard

From him I come

With message unto princely Pericles;

But since my landing I have understood

Your lord has betook himself to unknown travels,

My message must return from whence it came.

Helicanus

We have no reason to desire it,

Commended to our master, not to us:

Yet, ere you shall depart, this we desire,

As friends to Antioch, we may feast in Tyre. Exeunt.

questions.question: Why does Thaliard call his errand dangerous?
questions.questionKo: 탈리아드는 왜 제 임무를 위험하다 하는가?

options.text: Because the seas between Antioch and Tyre are stormy.
options.textKo: 안티오크와 티레 사이 바다가 험해서.

options.text: Because the lords of Tyre already know his face.
options.textKo: 티레의 귀족들이 이미 그의 얼굴을 알아서.

options.text: Here he must kill King Pericles, and if he does not do it he is sure to be hanged at home.
options.textKo: 여기서 페리클레스 왕을 죽여야 하고, 그러지 못하면 고향에서 목이 매달릴 것이 확실하므로.

options.text: Because he has lost the poison Antiochus gave him.
options.textKo: 안티오코스가 준 독을 잃어버려서.

questions.sourceSnippet: Here must I kill King Pericles; and if I do it not, I am sure to be hanged at home

questions.question: What lesson does Thaliard draw about serving a king?
questions.questionKo: 탈리아드가 왕을 섬기는 일에 대해 끌어내는 교훈은?

options.text: That a servant should always ask the reason for an order.
options.textKo: 하인은 언제나 명의 이유를 물어야 한다고.

options.text: That kings reward faithful men above all others.
options.textKo: 왕은 무엇보다 충직한 자에게 상을 준다고.

options.text: That secrets are the only safe currency at court.
options.textKo: 궁정에서 안전한 화폐는 비밀뿐이라고.

options.text: The wise fellow who, bid to ask what he would, desired to know none of the king’s secrets — for if a king bid a man be a villain, he is bound by his oath to be one.
options.textKo: 무엇이든 청하라 하자 왕의 비밀은 하나도 알지 않게 해 달라 한 그 지혜로운 자 — 왕이 악당이 되라 명하면 서약에 매여 악당이 되어야 하므로.

questions.sourceSnippet: for if a king bid a man be a villain, he’s bound by the indenture of his oath to be one

questions.question: What does Helicanus tell the lords about the king’s departure?
questions.questionKo: 헬리카누스는 왕의 출발에 대해 귀족들에게 무엇이라 하는가?

options.text: The sealed commission left in trust with him speaks sufficiently that Pericles is gone to travel.
options.textKo: 자기에게 맡겨진 봉인된 위임장이 페리클레스가 여행을 떠났음을 충분히 말해 준다고.

options.text: That the king has gone to Antioch to make peace.
options.textKo: 왕이 화친하러 안티오크로 갔다고.

options.text: That the king lies sick and may not be seen.
options.textKo: 왕이 병들어 누워 만날 수 없다고.

options.text: That he does not know where the king has gone.
options.textKo: 왕이 어디로 갔는지 자기도 모른다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: His seal’d commission, left in trust with me, Doth speak sufficiently he’s gone to travel

questions.question: What account does Helicanus give of why Pericles left?
questions.questionKo: 헬리카누스는 페리클레스가 떠난 이유를 어떻게 설명하는가?

options.text: That Antiochus threatened Tyre with war.
options.textKo: 안티오코스가 티레를 전쟁으로 위협했다고.

options.text: Royal Antiochus took some displeasure at him — at least he judged so; doubting he had erred, to show his sorrow he would correct himself, and so put himself to the shipman’s toil.
options.textKo: 안티오코스 왕이 그에게 언짢아했다고 — 적어도 그가 그리 여겼고, 제가 잘못했나 싶어 슬픔을 보이려 스스로를 바로잡고자 뱃사람의 고생길에 몸을 맡겼다고.

options.text: That the king went to seek a wife elsewhere.
options.textKo: 왕이 다른 데서 아내를 구하러 갔다고.

options.text: That the lords themselves had urged him to go.
options.textKo: 귀족들이 스스로 그에게 떠나라 권했다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: Took some displeasure at him; at least he judged so

questions.question: What does Thaliard conclude in his second aside?
questions.questionKo: 탈리아드가 두 번째 방백에서 내리는 결론은?

options.text: That he must sail after Pericles at once.
options.textKo: 당장 배를 타고 페리클레스를 뒤쫓아야겠다고.

options.text: That he will serve Helicanus instead of Antiochus.
options.textKo: 안티오코스 대신 헬리카누스를 섬기겠다고.

options.text: He shall not be hanged now, although he would — since Pericles escaped the land only to perish at sea.
options.textKo: 이제는 목이 매달릴 일이 없겠다고 — 페리클레스가 육지를 벗어나 봐야 바다에서 죽을 터이므로.

options.text: That he will confess everything to the lords of Tyre.
options.textKo: 티레의 귀족들에게 모든 것을 털어놓겠다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: He ’scaped the land, to perish at the sea

questions.question: How does Thaliard present himself once he steps forward?
questions.questionKo: 탈리아드는 앞으로 나서며 자신을 어떻게 소개하는가?

options.text: As a merchant of Antioch seeking trade in Tyre.
options.textKo: 티레에서 장사할 안티오크의 상인이라고.

options.text: As a physician sent to attend the sick king.
options.textKo: 병든 왕을 돌보러 보내진 의사라고.

options.text: He does not present himself and leaves in secret.
options.textKo: 나서지 않고 몰래 떠난다.

options.text: As coming from Antiochus with a message unto princely Pericles — which, the lord being gone, must return whence it came.
options.textKo: 안티오코스가 보낸 전갈을 페리클레스 왕자에게 전하러 왔다고 — 그 주인이 떠났으니 그 전갈은 온 곳으로 돌아가야 한다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: With message unto princely Pericles

questions.question: How does Helicanus answer Thaliard, and what does he propose?
questions.questionKo: 헬리카누스는 탈리아드에게 어떻게 답하며 무엇을 제안하는가?

options.text: They have no reason to desire the message, since it was commended to their master and not to them — but before he departs they would feast in Tyre as friends to Antioch.
options.textKo: 그 전갈은 자기들이 아니라 주인에게 맡겨진 것이니 알고 싶을 까닭이 없다고 — 다만 떠나기 전에 안티오크의 벗으로서 티레에서 잔치를 벌이자고.

options.text: He demands to read the message at once.
options.textKo: 당장 그 전갈을 읽어 보겠다고 요구한다.

options.text: He orders Thaliard seized and questioned.
options.textKo: 탈리아드를 붙잡아 심문하라 명한다.

options.text: He sends him away without a word of courtesy.
options.textKo: 예의 한마디 없이 돌려보낸다.

questions.sourceSnippet: As friends to Antioch, we may feast in Tyre
